verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You feel your mind racing without rest. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, and that holding it feels like holding the wind. This same restlessness can echo in your own thoughts today. When the noise rises, you might simply notice it as a strong force, without trying to grip it.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after hearing about the disciplined life. He admits that his own mind refuses to settle. It moves fast and fights back. He compares trying to control it to catching the wind. The verse accepts this difficulty. It says the mind is restless and stubborn by nature. That same restlessness is what you feel now. Your thoughts move fast and will not sit still.

verse_text.speaker: Sutikshna
verse_text.setting: The young sage Sutikshna hears Ram is coming and runs to meet him, full of doubt about himself.
verse_text.line: I have no devotion, no wisdom, no steady love. But he loves the one who has nowhere else to go.
verse_text.translation: 'Will Ram, my master, with his brother, meet me as he would his own servant? There is no firm trust in my heart; no devotion, detachment or wisdom in my mind; no good company, no yoga, chanting or sacrifice, no steady love for his lotus feet. But the ocean of compassion has one habit: the one who has no other refuge is dear to him.'

reading: You feel uneasy in your care for your parents. Sutikshna says he has no devotion, wisdom, or steady love, yet the compassionate one loves the person who has nowhere else to go. This speaks to you today: your own strength may feel absent, but your care itself places you in the refuge that is already held.
meaning: Sutikshna is a young sage. He hears that Ram is near and runs out to meet him. His heart is full of doubt. He thinks he has no devotion, no wisdom, and no steady love. He has no discipline and no good company. Yet he trusts one thing. He trusts that the ocean of compassion loves the one who has nowhere else to go. The verse says you do not have to feel qualified. You only have to be the one with no other refuge. Your care for your parents may feel unsteady right now. The verse says the one you serve already holds the place you stand in, even when you doubt your own strength.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: You feel lonely right now. Krishna tells Arjuna, "See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me." When you look at the world around you and your children, you can see the same presence there, and it means you are never truly alone or lost.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna stands between two armies and feels the weight of what he must do. Krishna is teaching him how to settle the mind through meditation. He tells Arjuna that a person who sees him in every being and sees every being within him will never be lost to him, and he will never be lost to that person. You carry a quiet loneliness while the house fills with your children's noise. This verse names a way to meet that feeling without pushing it away.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what becomes of someone who tries and fails; Krishna reassures him.
verse_text.line: What happens to someone who believes, tries, slips, and doesn't make it to the end?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: One who has faith but does not strive enough, whose mind falls away from yoga before reaching perfection, what end does he come to, Krishna?

reading: You feel stuck and can't get started. Arjuna asks Krishna what happens to someone who believes, tries, slips, and doesn't reach the end. This speaks to your studying today: even when your effort slackens and your mind strays, that uncertainty itself is part of the path you are on.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna what becomes of a person who starts with faith but does not push hard enough, and whose mind wanders from yoga before perfection is reached. Krishna answers that no sincere effort is ever lost. The person simply picks up again from where they left off, carrying forward whatever they have already built. Your studying feels blocked right now, and this tells you that the effort you have already put in still counts even when you cannot begin again today.

verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.

Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is stubborn and strong, as hard to hold as the wind. In the midst of your duties, this same wind moves through you, and you can simply notice its force without trying to grip it.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after hearing the path of steady discipline. He admits that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He compares trying to control it to grasping the wind. Krishna agrees that the mind is hard to hold, yet he proposes that practice and letting go gradually train it. Your mind races across work, children and parents without pause. The verse names that force directly instead of asking you to calm it by force.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: You feel restless in the middle of your studies. Bali looks at the window and says day and night bring the same chain of tasks again and again, and to a thinking person this feels like a mockery. Perhaps your mind, caught in this loop of classes and assignments, is echoing that same weariness. You might pause at your desk and simply notice the next task without letting it mock you, letting the rhythm be what it is.
meaning: Bali speaks this to himself. He is a demon king who has ruled the three worlds for ages. One day he sits by his window and notices that day follows night and the same tasks return again and again. He feels that for a thinking person this repetition is a mockery. The verse proposes that when life feels like a loop, the work is not to add more tasks but to master the mind that runs the loop. You are studying and the same cycle of classes and assignments is wearing you down. Bali names that weariness as a mockery felt by a thinking mind.

verse_text.speaker: Rama's attendant
verse_text.setting: Rama's attendants describe the prince's withdrawal to his worried father.
verse_text.line: He no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just goes quiet.
verse_text.translation: He doesn't light up at jokes, doesn't lose himself in pleasures, doesn't stay with his work; he just keeps silent.

reading: You feel empty. The Yoga Vasishtha records that Rama, though surrounded by court life, no longer lights up at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work; he just keeps silent. In your own studying, working, and caring, that same quiet withdrawal can be a sign that the old measures no longer hold your attention.
meaning: Rama's attendants speak to King Dasharatha after the prince returns from a long pilgrimage. Sixteen-year-old Rama has withdrawn from court life. He stops eating well, stops laughing, ignores his duties, and sits alone. The attendants tell the worried king that Rama no longer reacts to jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work. He simply keeps silent. The verse proposes that this loss of interest is not mere illness or weakness. It can be the first stirring of deeper questions, provided someone helps the young prince through it. In your studying, working, and caring, that same quiet withdrawal can signal that the old measures no longer hold your attention.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You feel anxious while studying. Krishna tells Arjuna that contact between the senses and their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain, which come and go and do not last. You can bear them patiently as they pass, like the next exam result arriving and then fading.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that the true Self never comes into being and never perishes. The body changes like old clothes. Sense contact brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These feelings arrive and depart. They do not remain. Arjuna must bear them with patience. Your anxiety is a passing wave in the body, not the whole of who you are.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: You carry a peaceful feeling even while running your own work and raising kids. Krishna tells Arjuna that the one whose happiness, delight and light are all within becomes free and reaches lasting peace. That inner ease can stay with you through the busy days ahead, right in the middle of your own workspace and home.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while teaching the yoga of knowledge. Arjuna has been asking about the nature of the wise person and lasting happiness. Krishna describes the one who sees clearly. He says this person keeps happiness, delight and light inside. Pleasures that begin and end cannot hold their joy. Because they look inward, they become one with Brahman and reach the peace of Brahman. That peaceful feeling you carry already belongs to this kind of inner steadiness. It can remain with you through your workday and your home.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: At a working stage filled with hope, you are open to what comes next. Lakshmana tells Ram that enthusiasm is powerful and that nothing in the world is out of reach for the one who has it. Let that steadiness guide your next step today, whether you are starting a task or choosing a direction.

You carry hope even now, and this verse meets that openness with the reminder that your own energy shapes what lies ahead.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: You feel angry right now while studying. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born, and from attachment comes desire, then anger. This verse names the path your mind may be on today: a thought about something has sparked wanting, and that wanting has hit a wall. Notice where your attention is fixed as you sit with your books.

When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From that attachment comes desire. When desire is blocked, anger follows. The verse proposes that steadiness begins with guarding where attention rests. Your anger right now while studying may have started with a thought that stuck, then a wanting that met a wall.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?

reading: You feel your mind is overthinking. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, and that holding it feels like holding the wind. This speaks to you today because your racing thoughts may feel just as hard to grasp while you are raising kids. Notice that even Arjuna found the mind difficult to steady; you can simply set down the effort to force it still, and return your attention to one small task in front of you.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the battlefield. He admits that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He says it is as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna answers that practice and letting go can train this mind. Your racing thoughts feel just as hard to grasp while you are raising kids. Even Arjuna found the mind difficult to steady.

These feelings come and go and do not last. He asks Arjuna to bear them patiently. The restlessness you carry now is not a permanent state. It moves through you like the weather Krishna describes, and it will pass.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: You carry a peaceful feeling while balancing studies, work, and caring for your parents. Krishna tells Arjuna that the person who is happy within, at ease within, and lit from within finds lasting freedom. Your own inner light can shine through all these duties today, bringing you that same steady ease.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while teaching the path of knowledge. He describes the person who sees clearly. This person keeps their happiness inside themselves. Their delight stays inside. Their light comes from within. Such a person becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman. You feel peaceful while you study, work, and look after your parents. That steady feeling is already inside you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

reading: You carry a hurt that keeps burning. Krishna tells Narada that harsh words from family churn his heart like a fire-stick, day after day. The words spoken close to you still sting, yet your own heart remains the fire-stick being churned. Notice where that fire still burns in your chest today.
meaning: Krishna speaks to the sage Narada after growing weary of feuds within his own clan. He admits that the harsh words spoken by his relatives churn his heart like someone rubbing a fire-stick, and the pain keeps burning him day after day. The verse proposes that in family conflict, the only effective weapon is not force but gentleness, patience and respect. The words from someone close to you still sting, and the burn has not faded. That ache is real, and it sits with you now.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people turn to the divine: those in distress, those seeking knowledge, those in need, and the wise. Your curiosity places you among them. Right now, your own studies and work can be the path you are already walking.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna stands between two armies and feels the weight of the moment. Krishna explains that four kinds of people turn toward the divine. These are the ones in distress, the ones who seek knowledge, the ones who need something, and the wise. He names them as good people who worship him. The point is that any reason that brings a person to this search is welcome. Your curiosity about these words places you in that same group. It does not matter that you are also studying and working and caring for others.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: You carry a hopeful heart while running your own work and raising your kids. Lakshman tells Ram that enthusiasm is powerful and there is no strength greater than it, so for the one who has it, nothing is out of reach. Let that truth meet your mornings today: the energy you already bring to your own thing can carry you into new beginnings.
meaning: Lakshman speaks to Ram at Lake Pampa after Sita has been taken. Spring surrounds them, and the beauty of the place only deepens Ram's grief. Lakshman tells him that enthusiasm is powerful and that no strength is greater than it. For the person who holds it, nothing in the world is out of reach. You are carrying hope while you run your own work and raise your children. Lakshman reminds Ram that his own energy can move mountains, and the same truth can meet your mornings today.

verse_text.speaker: Manu
verse_text.setting: Manu, offered any boon after years of austerity, hesitates to ask for what he truly wants.
verse_text.line: Like a poor man before the wishing tree, we hesitate to ask for what we really want.
verse_text.translation: Like a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in my heart.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile; one thing still hurts him.
verse_text.line: What hurt most was not the news, but that he didn't tell me himself.
verse_text.translation: Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation.

reading: You carry a hurt from someone close. Ram speaks plainly about his own pain: the king did not tell him himself about Bharata's coronation. That silence still burns him. Your own wound may sit in the same quiet place, unnamed by the one who caused it.
meaning: Ram speaks these words to Kaikeyi after he has accepted fourteen years in the forest. He has already agreed to leave Ayodhya without anger. Yet one thing still burns him. He tells her that the worst part was not the news itself. It was that his father did not tell him in person about Bharata's coronation. The hurt comes from the silence of the one who should have spoken. Your own wound may sit in the same quiet place, unnamed by the one who caused it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: Krishna starts earlier than the outburst. Dhyāyato viṣayān puṃsaḥ: when you keep dwelling on something, you get attached, attachment turns into wanting, and wanting that meets a wall turns into anger. By the time you snap, the fire has been building for a while.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: The narrator Sanjaya speaks these words. He describes the greatest archer of his time putting down his bow and sitting in the chariot, his mind sunk in sorrow. The Gita begins with someone who can't go on, and it stays with him for seventeen more chapters.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You feel grateful right now. The poet asks what generous austerity brought him this freedom to wander, simple food without humiliation, noble company, and learning that only brings calm. Your own studies and care for your parents sit within this same quiet space. Notice the gentle mind that stirs only slightly even while looking outward, and let that steadiness be your anchor today.
meaning: The poet Bhartrihari speaks these lines as he reflects on a life of quiet devotion. He looks at his freedom to move, his plain meals, the company of good people, and his learning that brings only calm. He wonders what past discipline earned him such gifts. The verse holds gratitude for a simple existence and a devotion that does not fight over which form of God is supreme. Your studies and your care for your parents sit inside this same quiet space. The poet names a life without struggle, and you are living part of that now.

verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: Arjuna says this, and he was the finest archer of his time. He admits his own mind won't obey him. If yours keeps replaying the same conversation at 2 a.m., you are in good company, and the Gita takes the problem seriously before it offers anything.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: Krishna calls these mātrā-sparśa: contacts, things that touch you and move on. A deadline, a bad week, a hard meeting. They hurt while they last, they pass, and Krishna asks you to bear them (titikṣasva) until they do.

verse_text.speaker: Rama's attendant
verse_text.setting: Rama's attendants describe the prince's withdrawal to his worried father.
verse_text.line: He no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just goes quiet.
verse_text.translation: He doesn't light up at jokes, doesn't lose himself in pleasures, doesn't stay with his work; he just keeps silent.

reading: You feel empty while running your own thing and raising kids. Rama's attendant tells King Dasharatha that the prince no longer lights up at jokes or stays with his work, but simply keeps silent. In the same way, this quiet withdrawal can point toward a deeper clarity rather than a failure.
meaning: Rama's attendant speaks to King Dasharatha after the prince returns from a long pilgrimage. Rama has stopped eating, laughing, and doing his duties. He sits alone and keeps silent. The attendant reports that Rama no longer lights up at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work. He just keeps quiet. Your own quiet withdrawal mirrors Rama's, and it can open a door to deeper questions instead of marking a collapse.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You feel grateful. The poet Bhartrihari asks what generous austerity brought him this freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, noble company, and learning whose only fruit is calm. This verse speaks to your present season by naming those quiet gifts as worthy of wonder. You might rest your attention on the simple meal before you today, or the calm that comes from a mind stirring only gently.
meaning: The poet Bhartrihari speaks to the reader from a place of worship of Shiva. He sits with a life stripped of struggle. He names four gifts. Freedom to wander without chains. Food taken without anyone looking down. Company of noble people. Learning that brings only calm. He then asks what generous austerity earned him this. The verse proposes that a simple life is not ordinary. It is the fruit of past discipline. The speaker gives thanks without comparing one form of God to another. In your retired season, this names the quiet gifts you already hold as worthy of wonder.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'On the Greatness of Time'.
verse_text.line: Same night, same day, the same tasks on repeat. We run in circles and call it living.
verse_text.translation: Thinking 'it is the same night again, the same day', creatures run about in vain, busy as ever with the tasks they have set going; with work full of the same repeated things, tormented by this round of existence, alas, out of delusion we feel no shame.

reading: You feel restless right now. Bhartrihari writes that creatures run about in vain, busy as ever with the same repeated tasks, tormented by this round. The verse sees this loop as delusion, not as your failure. When your own days blur into the same tasks on repeat, let that recognition be enough to pause the running.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines to the reader from his reflection on the greatness of Time. He watches creatures caught in their routines. They think it is the same night again, the same day, and they keep running about in vain, busy with the same tasks they started. Tormented by this round, they feel no shame because they are lost in delusion. Your restlessness comes from this same loop. The verse names it delusion, not your failure.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that contact between the senses and their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain, which come and go and do not last. You are feeling anxious right now as you study. This verse suggests that your anxiousness, like these sensations, passes and does not stay. Notice the next wave of study stress that arrives, and simply let it come and go without clinging to it.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that the senses meeting their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These sensations arrive and then leave. They do not stay forever. The teaching is that what you truly are outlasts every loss and every passing pain. Your anxiousness right now is one of those sensations. It comes and goes, and it does not stay forever.

verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: Arjuna says this, and he was the finest archer of his time. He admits his own mind won't obey him. If yours keeps replaying the same conversation at 2 a.m., you are in good company, and the Gita takes the problem seriously before it offers anything.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You feel overthinking. Krishna hears Arjuna say the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. In your own racing thoughts, that same stubborn force is at work. You can rest against it today, letting the wind move without forcing it into stillness.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after hearing about mastering the mind. He admits that his thoughts race and refuse to settle. He compares the effort to seizing the wind. Krishna does not deny this difficulty. He points to steady practice and release as the way to train it over time. Your own racing thoughts carry that same stubborn force. You do not have to force them into stillness right now.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You feel empty even while running your own thing, raising kids, and studying. Young Rama asks, "What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?" His words speak to your today: when nothing feels like it matters, you can simply let it be unreal and rest in the question of who you are.
meaning: Young Rama has just returned from his travels and sits in his father's court. The sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha are there with him. Rama tells them that nothing interests him anymore. He asks what kingship means to him and what pleasures are worth anything. He asks who he truly is and what all this is for. He says if the world is unreal then let it be unreal, and asks whose it is and what anyone has gained. You feel empty even while running your own thing, raising kids, and studying. Rama's question names that hollow space without rushing to fill it.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You feel grateful right now. The poet asks what generous austerity earned this freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, and living among noble people, along with learning whose only fruit is calm. Let this question remind you today of the simple, steady life you already hold.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines from his Worship of Shiva. He looks at his own life and sees freedom to move as he wishes, food that carries no shame, company that is noble, and learning that brings only calm. He wonders what generous austerity earned such gifts. He offers no rival worship between forms of God. He simply stands in wonder at a simple life lived without struggle. You carry gratitude for the steady life you already hold. Let this wonder at your own quiet fortune settle beside the work you do.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You feel overthinking right now. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, and that holding it feels like holding the wind. This speaks to your racing thoughts today: the mind can simply be turbulent, and you do not have to wrestle it into stillness. Let your breath be the anchor you return to, even as the thoughts blow past.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the battlefield. He admits that his mind refuses to settle. It moves fast and resists every attempt to pin it down. He compares the effort to catching the wind. Krishna agrees that the mind is restless and stubborn. He adds that steady practice and letting go can gradually train it. Your thoughts are not a signal that you are failing. They are simply turbulent, and they can settle with repetition rather than force.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: You feel mocked by the same tasks repeating day after day. Bali says, 'Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks... to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.' Your restless working life mirrors this endless loop. Notice one concrete task from today and simply set it down, letting the cycle pause for a breath.
meaning: King Bali sits by his window after ruling the three worlds for ages. He looks out and sees day follow night, task follow task, with no end in sight. He speaks this to himself. He says the same chain of duties repeats again and again. To a thinking person, this repetition feels like a mockery. You feel mocked by the same tasks repeating day after day. Bali's endless loop mirrors your restless working life.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: The narrator Sanjaya speaks these words. He describes the greatest archer of his time putting down his bow and sitting in the chariot, his mind sunk in sorrow. The Gita begins with someone who can't go on, and it stays with him for seventeen more chapters.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: You feel peaceful right now. Krishna tells Arjuna that the one who is happy within, at ease within, and lit from within finds lasting freedom. This points to a joy that does not depend on what is happening outside your studies. You can rest in that inner light today, letting it be the source of your calm.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while they stand on the battlefield. Arjuna is caught between duty and dread. Krishna describes the person who does not lean on outer events for joy. This person keeps happiness inside their own mind. They keep delight inside. They keep their light inside. When all three rest there, that yogi joins with Brahman. That yogi reaches the peace of Brahman. You feel peaceful right now. That inner calm is not a break from your studies. It is the same source Krishna points to. You can let it stay as your own ground today.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile; one thing still hurts him.
verse_text.line: What hurt most was not the news, but that he didn't tell me himself.
verse_text.translation: Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation.

reading: You carry a hurt that still burns. Ram tells Kaikeyi that the deepest pain was not the exile itself, but that his father did not tell him the news directly. Today, that silence from someone close may sit heavier than the blow. You can name that one sorrow plainly, without letting it consume the rest.
meaning: Ram has just agreed to leave for the forest for fourteen years. Kaikeyi has demanded this after securing a promise from his father. Ram accepts the exile without anger. Yet one thing wounds him. He tells Kaikeyi that the deepest pain is not the news of the exile. It is that his father did not tell him this himself. The person close to you has caused a wound. The sharper edge of that pain may be their silence, not only what they did.

verse_text.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse_text.setting: Letter from the USA, 9 July 1895, on opposition to his work in America.
verse_text.line: Each work has to pass through these stages — ridicule, opposition, and then acceptance.
verse_text.translation: Each work has to pass through these stages — ridicule, opposition, and then acceptance. Each man who thinks ahead of his time is sure to be misunderstood.

reading: You feel inspired as you step into this new chapter. Swami Vivekananda writes that every work passes through ridicule, opposition, and then acceptance. Your own resolve can carry you through the early resistance, just as his did, toward the acceptance that follows.
meaning: Swami Vivekananda writes from America to the Maharaja of Khetri. Some clergy there oppose his work. He tells his friend that any work moves through three stages. First comes ridicule. Then comes opposition. After that comes acceptance. He adds that anyone ahead of their time will be misunderstood. Your resolve meets early resistance. That resistance is a stage, not a final word on what you are building.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: You carry a hopeful heart as you move through your working years. Lakshman tells Ram that enthusiasm is powerful and there is no strength greater than it; for the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach. Let that steady energy guide your next step forward, starting with one small task today.
meaning: Lakshman speaks to Ram at Lake Pampa after Sita has been taken. Spring surrounds them, and the beauty of the place only deepens Ram's grief. Lakshman sees this and tells him that enthusiasm holds the greatest strength. For the one who carries it, no task in the world lies beyond reach. You are moving through your working years with a hopeful heart, and that hope can carry you even when the path ahead is unclear.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You carry a heavy sense of guilt. Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against their will, as if pushed by force. This verse names the struggle you feel today, showing that doing wrong while unwilling points to a force beyond your control. Let that recognition rest on the weight you are already carrying.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against their own will, as if pushed by some force. Krishna answers that unmet desire turns into anger, and this anger is the enemy that clouds a person's wisdom. The verse proposes that the person must see this force clearly and then master it. The guilt you carry points to a force that moves you against your own wish. Seeing it as desire turned sour can lift some of the weight from your own name.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: Krishna describes someone whose happiness, pleasure and light are all inside: antaḥ-sukhaḥ, antar-ārāmaḥ, antar-jyotiḥ. Good days still come from outside. This joy doesn't depend on them.
